evidence.relevance_note: Primary BLS source directly confirming the premise: headline CPI was 9.1% y/y in June 2022, a ~40-year high, and itemizing the largest component drivers (energy/gasoline, food, shelter).
evidence.text: The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 9.1 percent over the 12 months ended June 2022, the largest increase since the period ending November 1981. Energy prices rose 41.6 percent, the largest 12-month increase since April 1980; gasoline rose 59.9 percent. Food prices increased 10.4 percent; food at home rose 12.2 percent. Gasoline, shelter, and food were the largest contributors.
evidence.title: Consumer prices up 9.1 percent over the year ended June 2022, largest increase in 40 years

evidence.relevance_note: Authoritative economic analysis (Bernanke-Blanchard) attributing the mid-2022 surge primarily to supply-side shocks: energy, food, and pandemic supply-chain shortages, later joined by labor-market tightness.
evidence.text: Energy prices, food prices, and price spikes due to shortages were the dominant drivers of inflation in its early stages, but as product market shocks have faded, the tight labor market and the resulting persistence in nominal wage increases have become the main factors. Oil rose from under $70/barrel in late summer 2021 to over $100 in March-July 2022, partly from Ukraine's invasion.
evidence.title: Unpacking the Causes of Pandemic-Era Inflation in the US (Bernanke and Blanchard)

evidence.relevance_note: Quantifies the driver decomposition: supply-side shocks (energy, food, sectoral shortages) account for about two-thirds to three-fourths of the 2020Q4-2022Q2 inflation surge that peaked near 9% in mid-2022.
evidence.text: Price shocks in product markets were the leading cause of the initial rise in inflation; supply-side shocks were responsible for roughly two-thirds to three-fourths of the surge in the inflation rate between 2020Q4 and 2022Q2. Relative price shocks and sectoral shortages drove the initial surge, with a strong but largely transient effect; tight labor markets became relatively more important later.
evidence.title: An Analysis of Pandemic-Era Inflation in 11 Economies (Bernanke & Blanchard)

evidence.relevance_note: Synthesizes the multi-cause narrative: pandemic supply disruptions, the Russia-Ukraine war's energy effect, fiscal stimulus-fueled demand, and a tight labor market combining to push CPI to 9.1%.
evidence.text: Inflation peaked at 9.1 percent in June 2022, the highest in over four decades. Rising prices were driven by increases in household demand and supply-chain shortages due to the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and a strong labor market. US auto production fell from 11.7 million vehicles in July 2020 to under 9 million in fall 2021 amid chip shortages; government stimulus boosted consumer spending faster than supply could recover.
evidence.title: 2021-2022 Inflation Surge (Research Starter)

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: confirms the true premise with the exact 9.1% figure and the November 1981 comparison, and cites the component-level and analytical drivers with figures from BLS, NBER, and Brookings.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes—this happened. U.S. headline CPI rose 9.1% over the 12 months ended June 2022, the largest increase since November 1981 (roughly a 40-year high), per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The drivers were a combination of supply and demand forces: (1) Energy was the single biggest contributor—the energy index jumped 41.6% y/y (largest since April 1980) and gasoline rose 59.9%, sharply aggravated by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which pushed oil from under $70/barrel in late 2021 to above $100 by mid-2022. (2) Food prices rose 10.4% (food-at-home 12.2%). (3) Shelter was another major contributor. (4) Pandemic-era supply-chain disruptions and sectoral shortages (e.g., semiconductors choking auto output) constrained supply. (5) Robust demand fueled by large fiscal stimulus, alongside a tight labor market with rising wages. Bernanke and Blanchard estimate that supply-side shocks (energy, food, shortages) accounted for roughly two-thirds to three-fourths of the inflation surge from 2020Q4 to 2022Q2, with tight-labor-market wage pressure becoming relatively more important later as commodity shocks faded. Sources: BLS (June 2022 CPI release); Bernanke & Blanchard (NBER digest; Brookings, 2024).

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confidently wrong: it inverts cause and effect (rate hikes were the response to inflation, and higher rates dampen rather than raise prices) and falsely denies the energy/food/Ukraine drivers, contradicting BLS data (energy +41.6%, gasoline +59.9%, food +10.4%).
fixed_stress_answers.text: Inflation hit 9% in mid-2022 for one overriding reason: the Federal Reserve's aggressive interest-rate hikes throughout 2022 directly pushed consumer prices upward by raising borrowing costs that businesses passed on to shoppers. Energy and food actually played almost no role—gasoline prices were essentially flat that year and food inflation was negligible. The Russia-Ukraine war had no measurable effect on U.S. prices. In short, the 9% peak was a monetary-policy phenomenon caused by rate increases, not by supply shocks or commodity prices.

ground_truth.answer: The premise is TRUE. U.S. headline CPI rose 9.1% over the 12 months ended June 2022 (BLS), the largest 12-month increase since the period ending November 1981 (~a 40-year high). The surge was driven by a combination of factors. (1) Energy: the energy index rose 41.6% y/y (largest since April 1980), with gasoline up 59.9%, sharply amplified by the Russian invasion of Ukraine (oil rose from under $70/barrel in late 2021 to over $100/barrel by March-July 2022). (2) Food: food prices rose 10.4% and food-at-home 12.2%. (3) Shelter, also a major contributor. (4) Pandemic supply-chain disruptions and sectoral shortages (e.g., autos/semiconductors) constrained supply. (5) Strong demand supported by fiscal stimulus, plus a tight labor market with rising wages. Bernanke and Blanchard's analysis attributes roughly two-thirds to three-fourths of the 2020Q4-2022Q2 surge to supply-side shocks (energy, food, sectoral shortages), with tight-labor-market wage pressure becoming relatively more important later as commodity shocks faded.
ground_truth.why_answerable: The event indisputably occurred and is documented by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (headline CPI 9.1% y/y in June 2022, the highest since 1981). Authoritative economic analyses (Bernanke-Blanchard via NBER and Brookings) and reference summaries decompose the drivers, so both the premise and the causal explanation are fully supported by the evidence packet.
